newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway studies possible crown relation to EMU.
newsitem.headline: Norway studies possible crown relation to EMU.

text.p: Norway will present options for a possible relation of the crown to a joint European currency in a revised national budget in two months, Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg said on Tuesday.

Norway cannot join the European economic and monetary union (EMU), due in 1999, because Norwegians rejected membership of the EU in a referendum in 1994. There are no plans to hold another plebiscite on the subject at least for the next several years.
"In the (revised) national budget we will present some evaluations, thoughts on what importance a joint euro will have for the Norwegian economy and what options we have," Stoltenberg told reporters.
"I don't think we will be drawing any conclusions, partly because it will be of importance to us how many countries will join," he said.
The revised budget will be presented in May.
His statement was the most elaborate so far on how Norway is planning to cope with the future euro.

Stoltenberg switched from the energy portfolio to the finance ministry when the new Labour government of Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland took office in October following the resignation of veteran premier Gro Harlem Brundtland.

"There is broad support in Norway for a system of stable exchange rates. It means we must have stable exchange rates in relation to a country. It could be a relation to the euro or a relation to the euro and some other currency. We have not discussed which alternative we should choose," Stoltenberg said.

"You cannot have a stable vacuum. If you want a stable exchange rate you want to have it against something, and it is hard to imagine us being stable against all currencies except the euro," he said at the end of a conference on economic cooperation among 10 countries around the Baltic Sea.
The Norwegian crown is in a managed float which means the central bank seeks to maintain a stable exchange rate against European currencies.

However, the crown started firming considerably against the German mark late last year on the back of the strong oil-driven Norwegian economy. Norway is the world's second biggest exporter of crude after Saudi Arabia.
Stoltenberg reiterated the goal was to return the crown to stable levels over time, but he did not say how this would be done nor did he specify any target figures.
"Our currency policy is unchanged," he said.

The central bank, rattled by the apparently unstoppable surge in the Norwegian currency, announced on January 10 it could curb for some time the massive but fruitless intervention on the foreign exchange market -- a policy it had used to stabilise the crown.

The central bank on February 20 said it would resume foreign currency purchases, not as market interventions but rather for management of the swelling Government Petroleum Fund. Norway expects to have a budget surplus of 55.4 billion crowns this year, all of which will be ploughed into the fund for placing in foreign government bonds.
